people.name: Rene Madrid
body: On Lake Street in Minneapolis, which Twin Cities Business calls one of the region's most diverse corridors, a small business owner can walk into a U.S. Bank branch looking for a loan, a checking account, or advice. For more than a decade, the person running that branch has been Rene Madrid, an immigrant from El Salvador. The magazine says his own experience as an immigrant fuels his work on financial inclusion.

Madrid has spent nearly 30 years in the financial industry. As vice president and branch manager, he focuses on helping small businesses and widening access to financial tools. He has worked with local schools, cultural groups, and a Latino economic development organization.

His work also reaches the next generation. Over the past 15 years he has mentored more than 65 high school students, with attention to professional confidence: how to present yourself and how to speak up at work.
In 2026 Twin Cities Business named him one of its Notable Diverse Leaders. His story is one of steady work inside an everyday institution, the kind of contribution that seldom makes headlines.

Nearly 30 years in the financial industry.
Vice president and branch manager, U.S. Bank Lake Street branch, Minneapolis, for more than a decade.
Has mentored more than 65 high school students over 15 years.
2026: Named a Twin Cities Business Notable Diverse Leader.

people.name: Edwin Torres DeSantiago
body: Edwin Torres DeSantiago was born in El Salvador and was a first-generation student. He has built a career around making sure immigrant voices are heard in legislative and political work.

In 2024 Twin Cities Business named him one of its Notable Nonprofit Board Members. It listed him as vice president of public affairs at NewPublica, a Minneapolis communications firm, and as a board member of COPAL MN (Communities Organizing Latine Power and Action; Twin Cities Business gave the Spanish name Comunidades Organizando el Poder y la Acción Latina), a Minneapolis organization that mobilizes the Latino community for social, political and economic change. For COPAL he has spoken at community events, met with members, and connected the organization with funders and donors.

Board member, COPAL MN, Minneapolis, as listed in 2024.

people.name: Sandra Benítez
body: Sandra Benítez was born in Washington, D.C. She was raised in San Salvador, where her father worked at the U.S. Embassy, until she was sent to the United States for school at 14. Decades later, living in Minnesota, she turned to fiction with Latin American themes.

She was born Sandra Jeannette Ables (the spelling El Diario de Hoy gives) on March 26, 1941. Minnesota Writers on the Map says she adopted her mother's maiden name, Benítez. She attended high school and college in Missouri, earning a bachelor's degree in education and a master's in comparative literature at Northeast Missouri State University, now Truman State. In 1979, in midlife, she left a job translating management training manuals and took a creative writing course.

Her first novel, A Place Where the Sea Remembers (1993), won the 1994 Minnesota Fiction Award. Bitter Grounds (1997) won the 1998 American Book Award. Other books include The Weight of All Things, Night of the Radishes, and the memoir Bag Lady, about living with ulcerative colitis.

She received a 2004 National Hispanic Heritage Award for Literature, and in 2006 she was named one of the first United States Artists fellows. She made her home in Minnesota. By El Diario de Hoy's account, she died in Minneapolis on July 25, 2024.
keyFacts: 1941: Born in Washington, D.C.; raised in San Salvador until age 14.
1979: Took her first creative writing course.
1993: A Place Where the Sea Remembers; 1994 Minnesota Fiction Award.
1997: Bitter Grounds; 1998 American Book Award.
2006: Named one of the first United States Artists fellows.
2024: Died July 25.

people.name: Frank Rubio
body: On September 27, 2023, a Soyuz capsule landed in Kazakhstan, bringing NASA astronaut Frank Rubio home after 371 days in orbit. NASA says no U.S. astronaut had spent that long on a single spaceflight. The mission had been planned to last about six months.

Rubio's family story runs through El Salvador. NASA gives his birthplace as Los Angeles, says he considers Miami his hometown, and notes that his mother, Myrna Argueta, lives in El Salvador. He was born in December 1975 to Salvadoran parents, and Voice of America reports that he lived in El Salvador for his first six years before the family moved to Miami.

He graduated from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1998. As an Army aviator he flew UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters for more than 1,100 hours, including more than 600 hours of combat and imminent-danger time. He then earned a medical degree from the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences in 2010. He is a family physician and Army flight surgeon, and he holds the rank of colonel.

NASA selected him in its 2017 astronaut candidate class. He launched on Soyuz MS-22 on September 21, 2022, and made three spacewalks. As of October 2026, NASA lists him as a mission specialist for Artemis III, which it describes as a low Earth orbit mission testing rendezvous and docking between Orion and commercial spacecraft.
keyFacts: 1998: Graduated from West Point.
More than 1,100 Black Hawk flight hours, including over 600 combat or imminent-danger hours.
2010: Medical degree, Uniformed Services University.
2017: Selected as a NASA astronaut candidate.
September 21, 2022 to September 27, 2023: 371 days, the longest single spaceflight by a U.S. astronaut.
As of October 2026: Assigned as a mission specialist for Artemis III.
people.connectToWork: Does your intake leave room for a person who was born in one country, raised in another and has family in a third? What would you ask rather than infer from a birthplace?

people.name: George Meléndez Wright
body: In 1929 a 25-year-old biologist set out with a small crew to survey the wildlife of about 14 western national parks, paying for the work himself, including his colleagues' salaries. George Meléndez Wright's survey changed how the United States manages its parks. He argued that parks should protect wild animals and the places they live, not only scenery.

Wright was born in San Francisco on June 20, 1904. His mother, Mercedes Meléndez, was born in San Salvador, and the National Park Service says her family had great political influence in El Salvador, where two of his uncles served as president. His parents died when he was young, and he was raised by his step-grandmother. He entered the University of California, Berkeley, at 16 and graduated in forestry in 1927. He then joined the Park Service at Yosemite. Review excerpts for a recent biography call him the first Hispanic person in a professional position in the agency.

His survey produced Fauna of the National Parks of the United States, published in 1933, and a second report, Wildlife Management in the National Parks, in 1934. The Park Service adopted the second report as official policy. In 1933 Wright became the first chief of its new Wildlife Division.

In February 1936 Wright died after a car crash near Deming, New Mexico, while returning from an expedition to what is now Big Bend National Park. Yellowstone Superintendent Roger Toll died with him. Wright was 31.
keyFacts: 1904: Born June 20 in San Francisco to a mother born in San Salvador.
1929: Began a self-funded wildlife survey of western national parks.
1933: Became the first chief of the Park Service's Wildlife Division.
1934: Wildlife Management in the National Parks adopted as Park Service policy.
1936: Died in February after a car crash near Deming, New Mexico.
people.connectToWork: Whose history does your team count as recent, and whose as long-standing? How could that assumption shape who you plan for?

people.name: Ana Sol Gutiérrez
body: When Ana Sol Gutiérrez won a seat on the Montgomery County, Maryland, Board of Education in 1990, the Maryland Women's Hall of Fame says she became the first Salvadoran American elected to public office in the United States.

She was born on January 11, 1942, in Santa Ana, El Salvador. Her family settled in Silver Spring, Maryland, when her father was appointed one of the founding directors of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. She graduated from Bethesda-Chevy Chase High School in 1960 and earned a B.S. in chemistry from Pennsylvania State University in 1964. She went on to earn a master's degree from American University and did graduate work in applied engineering at George Washington University.

She served on the school board from 1990 to 1998, including a term as president in 1995–96. In 2002 she was elected to the Maryland House of Delegates, where she represented District 18 from 2003 to 2019. The Hall of Fame credits her as the first Latina elected to public office in Montgomery County and in Maryland. In 2016 she ran in the Democratic primary for Maryland's 8th Congressional District and finished fourth with 5.5 percent of the vote. In 2018 she ran for the Montgomery County Council and lost.
As of April 2026 she was still taking part in county politics, publicly backing a candidate for county executive.
keyFacts: 1942: Born January 11 in Santa Ana, El Salvador.
1964: B.S. in chemistry, Pennsylvania State University.
1990–1998: Montgomery County Board of Education; president 1995–96.
2003–2019: Maryland House of Delegates, District 18.
2016: Finished fourth in the Democratic primary for Maryland's 8th Congressional District.

people.name: Hugo Pérez
body: Hugo Pérez was born in El Salvador on November 8, 1963, and became a leading U.S. soccer player years before the sport had its present top professional league in the United States.

He played for the United States at the 1984 Summer Olympics and for the U.S. men's national team from 1984 to 1994, earning 73 caps and scoring 13 goals. He missed the 1990 World Cup because of an injury suffered while playing in the French second division. Late in his career he played two seasons for FAS of Santa Ana in El Salvador before retiring in 1996.

In 2008 he was elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame. Later he returned to his birth country as a coach. He coached El Salvador's under-23 team and then took over the senior national team in April 2021. In September 2023, after a run of matches without a win and an argument with a journalist, the Salvadoran federation said it was ending his contract.

1984: U.S. Olympic soccer team.
1984–1994: 73 caps and 13 goals for the U.S. men's national team.

2021–2023: Head coach of El Salvador's national team.

people.name: Javier Zamora
body: Javier Zamora was born in La Herradura, El Salvador, in 1990. When he was nine, he traveled north through Guatemala, Mexico and the Sonoran Desert to be reunited with his parents in the United States. His parents had migrated ahead of him. The journey took about two months.

Zamora later turned that journey into literature. His poetry collection Unaccompanied (2017, Copper Canyon Press) explores family separation, war and the border. His memoir Solito (2022, Hogarth) tells the story of his childhood crossing through the eyes of a nine-year-old.

His honors include a Wallace Stegner Fellowship at Stanford (2016–18), a Lannan Literary Fellowship (2017), a Radcliffe Institute fellowship at Harvard (2018–19), and a 2024 Whiting Award in nonfiction.
His work puts one person's life behind the phrase "unaccompanied minor."
keyFacts: 1990: Born in La Herradura, El Salvador.
At age nine: Traveled to the U.S. to rejoin his parents.
2017: Unaccompanied (Copper Canyon Press).
2022: Solito (Hogarth).

people.name: Julio Torres
body: Julio Torres was born in El Salvador in the late 1980s. In 2009 he moved to New York to attend college at The New School, and he became a comedy writer known for absurd, imaginative work.

Beginning in 2016 he wrote for Saturday Night Live for several seasons. His best-known sketch there is "Papyrus," a short film in which Ryan Gosling plays a man obsessed with the font used in the Avatar logo. He has been nominated five times for the Emmy for Outstanding Writing for a Variety Series as part of the SNL writing team. With Fred Armisen and Ana Fabrega he co-created the largely Spanish-language HBO series Los Espookys (2019–2022), which won a 2022 Peabody Award.

His first feature film, Problemista (A24, 2024), which he wrote, directed and starred in, follows a young Salvadoran toy maker in New York trying to build a creative career before his work visa runs out.
keyFacts: Born in El Salvador; moved to New York in 2009.
2016: Began writing for Saturday Night Live.
2019: Los Espookys premiered on HBO; 2022 Peabody Award.

people.name: Christy Turlington Burns
body: In 2003 Christy Turlington gave birth to her first child and had complications. By then she was one of the most famous faces in the world. The experience led her to maternal health, the work she is now best known for.

She was born on January 2, 1969, in California. Her mother was a flight attendant from El Salvador, and her father was a Pan Am pilot. Turlington became a leading model, and at 20 she signed an exclusive three-year contract with Calvin Klein. In a 2013 interview she recalled sitting for the sculptor of mannequins for the Metropolitan Museum's 1993 Costume Institute exhibition.

She also went back to school. She earned a bachelor's degree cum laude from New York University's Gallatin School, and she later studied public health at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health. In 2005 she became a maternal health advocate for CARE, and the Skoll Foundation says she has supported efforts to rebuild post-war El Salvador since the 1990s.

In 2010 she made her directing debut with No Woman, No Cry, a documentary about maternal health that premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival. The same year she launched Every Mother Counts, a nonprofit working to make pregnancy and childbirth safe. As of October 2026, the organization calls her its founder and president.

Age 20: Signed an exclusive contract with Calvin Klein.
B.A. cum laude, NYU Gallatin School; studied public health at Columbia's Mailman School.
2005: Became a maternal health advocate for CARE.
2010: Directed No Woman, No Cry; launched Every Mother Counts.

people.name: Mario Bencastro
body: In 1979 Mario Bencastro was in Washington, D.C., preparing an exhibition of his paintings when he heard on the radio that there had been a coup in El Salvador. At that point he was an award-winning painter known for geometric, abstract work. The news from home turned him toward a different art form. He began writing a novel, a project that took about ten years.

That novel, Disparo en la catedral, was entered in Mexico's Diana International Literary Prize contest in 1989. It was a finalist and was first published in Mexico in 1990. Arte Público Press later published it in English as A Shot in the Cathedral (1996). Arte Público also published his stories of the civil war, The Tree of Life (1997).

His best-known novel, Odyssey to the North, follows Calixto, a migrant who travels north seeking work and safety from political persecution. The story is told through conversations, court transcripts, newspaper clippings and letters, and it shows immigrants in restaurant kitchens, courtrooms and detention centers. Arte Público also published his young-adult novel A Promise to Keep (2005) and the story collection Paraíso portátil / Portable Paradise (2010).
He is a native of El Salvador and has spoken with students at U.S. universities, including the University of North Carolina Wilmington in 2012.

1979: Learned of the coup in El Salvador while preparing a painting show in Washington, D.C.

people.name: Roberto Lovato
body: Roberto Lovato is a journalist, educator and author, born in 1963 and raised in the San Francisco Bay Area. Both of his parents were born in El Salvador. For years he set out to understand his family's past, and that search took him back to El Salvador.

The result was Unforgetting: A Memoir of Family, Migration, Gangs, and Revolution in the Americas, published by HarperCollins in 2020. The book reaches back to his father's childhood under the U.S.-backed Martínez dictatorship of the 1930s and carries forward to the present, when his father is an elderly man living with dementia. Along the way it covers El Salvador's civil war, mass migration and gang violence, and it ties the histories of the United States and El Salvador together.
The book was a New York Times Editors' Choice, a Newsweek "must read" of 2020, and one of the Los Angeles Times' best books of 2020.

His journalism has appeared in the New York Times, the Guardian and Der Spiegel, among others, and he received a reporting grant from the Pulitzer Center. He is the founder and lead strategist of #DignidadLiteraria, a campaign that won commitments to Latinx writers from Macmillan and other major U.S. publishers. As of October 2026 he is listed as an assistant professor of English at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

2020: Unforgetting (HarperCollins).
Pulitzer Center reporting grant.

people.name: Steve Montenegro
body: In January 2025 Steve Montenegro was serving as Speaker of the Arizona House of Representatives when the 57th Legislature opened, the first Hispanic Speaker in the chamber's history. He is a first-generation immigrant from El Salvador whose family fled the country's civil war for the United States in 1986.

Montenegro was first elected to the Arizona House in 2008, at age 27, and served there from 2009 to 2017. He rose to speaker pro tem in 2011 and was elected House majority leader in 2015. He then moved to the Arizona Senate, and on December 15, 2017, he resigned that seat to run for Congress in the 8th District after Trent Franks resigned. He lost the Republican primary in 2018.

He returned to the Arizona House in 2023 and was chosen as Speaker by the Republican caucus on November 12, 2024. As of October 2026 the Legislature's roster lists him as Speaker, a Republican from District 29. He is on the November 3, 2026, ballot for that district.

As with other elected officials, his positions draw both support and criticism. Read beside Ana Sol Gutiérrez and Wendy Carrillo, his career shows Salvadoran Americans holding public office in different parties.

2025: First Hispanic Speaker of the Arizona House.

people.name: Claudia Castro Luna
body: In 2015 Seattle named Claudia Castro Luna its first Civic Poet, a post she held for about two years. She was then appointed Washington State Poet Laureate, serving from 2018 to 2021. In 2019 the Academy of American Poets named her one of its Poet Laureate Fellows.
Castro Luna was born in El Salvador. She earned a BA in anthropology from UC Irvine, an MA in urban planning from UCLA, and an MFA in poetry from Mills College.

Her books include the chapbook This City (Floating Bridge Press, 2016), Killing Marías (Two Sylvias Press, 2017), One River, A Thousand Voices (Chin Music Press, 2020), and Cipota Under the Moon (Tia Chucha Press, 2022). By its publisher's account, Killing Marías addresses each poem to a woman named María who was killed in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. Her memoir, The Flowers Along the Way, is announced as coming from Curbstone Press.
As of October 2026 she teaches at Seattle University's Matteo Ricci Institute and is on the Humanities Washington Speakers Bureau for 2025 to 2027.

people.name: Wendy Carrillo
body: Before Wendy Carrillo held public office, she was a Los Angeles radio host, reporter and producer. She went on to work in media and labor communications, and in 2017 she won a seat in the California State Assembly.

Carrillo was born in El Salvador and came to the United States as a young child. She grew up in Boyle Heights and City Terrace, graduated from Roosevelt High School, and studied at East Los Angeles College before earning a bachelor's degree from Cal State LA in 2005 and a master's degree from USC.

Her media career covered culture, human rights, global conflict and U.S. politics. She also led communications for a Los Angeles local of the Service Employees International Union and worked as a communications deputy for the Los Angeles City Council.

On December 5, 2017, she won a special runoff election for the 51st Assembly District, defeating fellow Democrat Luis López to succeed Jimmy Gomez, who had moved to Congress. She later represented the 52nd District, and she was re-elected in 2018, 2020 and 2022, serving through 2024. She ran for the Los Angeles City Council in the 2024 cycle and lost. In the June 2, 2026, primary for California State Senate District 26 she received 13.7 percent of the vote and did not advance to November.

people.name: Wendy Caishpal
body: At 14, Wendy Beatriz Caishpal Jaco was shot five times during an armed assault in El Salvador, and she has used a wheelchair since. She went on to earn a degree in legal sciences from Universidad Panamericana and works as a lawyer. She founded Ahuachapán sin Barreras ("Ahuachapán Without Barriers"), an inclusion organization that ran for more than ten years. NPR reported in 2019 that the group helped make city parks in Ahuachapán accessible and held pool parties for children with disabilities. It also ran a sign language diploma course she designed.

She later became executive director of the Red de Sobrevivientes y Personas con Discapacidad, a network she first joined as a participant. Today she works as an independent inclusion consultant, is a mother of two sons, and is the Salvadoran ambassador for the Humanium Metal project, which supports survivors of armed violence. The BBC named her one of its 100 Women in 2020.
She told NPR that after her first child was born, a doctor asked her to sign a form authorizing her sterilization. She refused. "I was able to defend myself because I knew about my rights," she said.

She speaks against treating disabled women as eternas niñas, "eternal girls," and she urges families to acompañar sin encerrar, to support without shutting a person in. She lives in El Salvador and is not a Salvadoran American.
keyFacts: Shot at 14; wheelchair user.
Lawyer, Universidad Panamericana; founder of Ahuachapán sin Barreras.
Former executive director, Red de Sobrevivientes y Personas con Discapacidad.
2019: Took part in a Mobility International USA leadership program in Oregon.
2020: BBC 100 Women. Humanium Metal ambassador in El Salvador.
people.connectToWork: When a health or service decision is put in front of a disabled person, how do you make sure they know their rights and that the decision is theirs?

people.name: Jenny Chinchilla
body: Jenny Chinchilla is a Salvadoran wheelchair user who was reported in 2022 as a project advisor at the Fundación Buceo Inclusivo (Inclusive Diving Foundation). In December 2022 the foundation held an inclusive diving event in Ayutuxtepeque for the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, to fulfill the wish of three young people who wanted to dive. Chinchilla says getting into the water helps people overcome their fears and the taboos that society, and sometimes their own families, place on people with disabilities. She is based in El Salvador and is not a Salvadoran American.
keyFacts: Wheelchair user; project advisor, Fundación Buceo Inclusivo, El Salvador, as reported in 2022.
December 2022: Inclusive diving event, Ayutuxtepeque.
people.connectToWork: Does the support you offer include recreation and things a person wants to try, or only what is judged necessary? How would you ask?

sources.label: Vórtice, Universidad Francisco Gavidia, "Con el buceo inclusivo, eliminamos barreras" (Dec. 13, 2022)

photo.alt: Jenny Chinchilla in sunglasses and a light top, seated in her wheelchair on a sandy beach and smiling toward the sea.

institutions.name: CARECEN Los Angeles
aliases: Central American Resource Center Los Angeles
institutions.type: Immigrant legal services and community organizing nonprofit
institutions.location: 2845 West 7th Street, Los Angeles; offices also in Van Nuys and San Bernardino
body: In 1983, Salvadoran refugees in Los Angeles founded the Central American Resource Center, determined to secure legal status for Central Americans fleeing civil war. It is one of a family of CARECEN organizations.

Today CARECEN describes its mission as defending human and civil rights for Central Americans and all immigrants, working for social and economic fairness, and celebrating cultural diversity. It calls itself the largest Central American immigrant rights organization in the country. It offers affordable immigration legal services; education and leadership programs; organizing and advocacy; and a Day Labor Center.
CARECEN says about 25,000 people use its services each year and that its Day Labor Center serves more than 120 people a day.
keyFacts: 1983: Founded by Salvadoran refugees in Los Angeles.
Services: immigration legal aid, youth and adult programs, advocacy, Day Labor Center.
Says it serves about 25,000 people a year.
Three legal offices: Los Angeles, Van Nuys, San Bernardino.
institutions.connectToWork: Which organizations did people build for themselves because no service existed? How would you learn from them, and who pays for their time?

sources.label: CARECEN Los Angeles, "About"
CARECEN Washington, D.C.

institutions.name: CARECEN Washington, D.C.
institutions.type: Latino immigrant services and civic engagement nonprofit
institutions.location: 1460 Columbia Road NW, Washington, D.C.; also Bladensburg, Maryland
body: CARECEN Washington, D.C., was founded in 1981 as the Central American Refugee Center, to protect the rights of refugees fleeing conflict in Central America. It began as a direct legal service agency and was incorporated in 1982.

Its website honors Joaquín Domínguez Parada as a founding visionary and reports that he died on June 26, 2025, in San Salvador. Today it provides housing, citizenship and immigration services, along with civic engagement and advocacy. By its own count, in 2025 it handled 1,233 legal cases, saw 44 people naturalized, and provided 1,309 housing services and counseling sessions. It also produces Radio CARECEN DC, a podcast.
In 2022 it responded when Washington began receiving buses of migrants and asylum seekers from Texas and Arizona. Its sister organizations include CARECEN Los Angeles, New York and San Francisco.
keyFacts: 1981: Founded as the Central American Refugee Center.
Founding visionary: Joaquín Domínguez Parada, who died June 26, 2025.
Services: housing, citizenship, immigration legal help, Radio CARECEN DC.
2022: Responded to migrant buses from Texas and Arizona.
institutions.connectToWork: Could someone get housing help and immigration help in your area without telling their story twice? Who connects those services now?

sources.label: CARECEN Washington, D.C.
CARECEN Washington, D.C., "History"

institutions.name: Salvadoran American Leadership and Educational Fund
body: In 1995, Carlos Vaquerano and a group of friends in Los Angeles founded La Organización Salvadoreña Americana. At first it served Salvadorans and Salvadoran Americans who needed immigration services, English classes or social services. In 1998 it was renamed the Salvadoran American Leadership and Educational Fund.
Since then SALEF has focused on education and political empowerment. It reports awarding more than 1,500 scholarships to underserved Salvadoran and other Latino students. It marked 30 years in 2025.
keyFacts: 1995: Founded by Carlos Vaquerano and friends.
1998: Renamed SALEF.
Reports more than 1,500 scholarships awarded.
Focus: education and political empowerment.
institutions.connectToWork: What do people in the communities you serve want for the next generation? How do your programs ask, rather than start from what is going wrong?

sources.label: SALEF, "Our History"
NBC Los Angeles, "NBC4 Supports SALEF" (2013)

institutions.name: Fundación Red de Sobrevivientes y Personas con Discapacidad
aliases: Network of Survivors and People with Disabilities
body: The Landmine Survivors Network was founded internationally in 1995 by two landmine survivors. Its El Salvador office opened in 2001, and a 2008 account by one of its fellows reported that it planned to become the Network of Survivors and People with Disabilities in 2009, widening its focus to all people with disabilities.

The same account says the office worked in health, economic opportunity and human rights, and took part in the push for the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. El Salvador ratified the Convention in October 2007 and became bound by it in May 2008. Wendy Caishpal, profiled on this page, later served as executive director. Its current programs could not be confirmed.
keyFacts: 2001: El Salvador office opened.
2009: Planned change to its present name and wider focus.
Focused on peer support, health, work and rights.
Based in El Salvador, not Minnesota.
institutions.connectToWork: If someone arrives with experience of disability rights work in another country, how would your service use what they already know?

sources.label: Larissa Hotra, Upside Down World, "A Recent History of the Disability Rights Movement in El Salvador" (July 18, 2008)
El Diario de Hoy, "Wendy Caishpal, la mujer que convirtió el dolor en fuerza y luz" (2025)

institutions.name: Fundación Sendas
body: Fundación Sendas is a disability rights organization that says it works throughout El Salvador. Its stated mission is to monitor whether the rights of persons with disabilities are respected, so that disabled people can empower themselves and drive social change. It trains disabled people and their families in their rights, with a focus on women and girls. It also does political advocacy with local and national government, and public awareness work. Its site does not give a founding year or founders.
keyFacts: Works across El Salvador: rights training, advocacy and public awareness.
Focus on women and girls with disabilities.
Based in El Salvador, not Minnesota.
institutions.connectToWork: Do women and girls with disabilities in your service hear about their rights directly, and not only through someone else? How do you know?

Fundación Sendas, "About"

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Salvadoran means people with ties to El Salvador, by birth, family or upbringing, who differ widely in generation, region, faith, education, language and when and why they or their families came. No peer-reviewed study focused only on Salvadoran families and disability was found, and no Minnesota study. What exists is mostly about Salvadoran and Central American immigrants' mental health after war and violence, or about Latinx parents in general. Each study below says who it covers.
questions: Can you tell me how this disability or condition started, if you would like to? You do not need to share anything you would rather not.
What words do you use for what you are experiencing? If you use a word such as nervios, what does it feel like or look like for you?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Did you agree with it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a disability label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who in your family helps, and who do you want to be part of decisions?
What would help you do more on your own, and what would you like to keep doing with others?
Is a church or faith community part of your support? Would you like them involved?
Do you have any worries about using services that I can help answer?
Which language or Spanish do you prefer, and does anyone in your family speak an Indigenous language?

context.heading: War, armed violence and disability in El Salvador
body: A 2008 account by a fellow at the Landmine Survivors Network in El Salvador reports that about 70,000 people were killed in the 12-year armed conflict and, citing Landmine Monitor, that roughly 300,000 were disabled by it. These are estimates. The same account says the 2008 census counted 4.1 percent of residents as living with a disability, or 235,302 of 5,744,113, and that the national human rights ombudsman's disability panel disputed that figure and put the share at 10 percent or higher.

For some people, then, disability may be connected to war, landmines or later armed violence, and for others it may not. Wendy Caishpal, profiled on this page, became disabled through armed violence. Ask what produced an impairment only as a question the person may choose to answer.

sources.label: Larissa Hotra, Upside Down World, "A Recent History of the Disability Rights Movement in El Salvador" (July 18, 2008)
El Diario de Hoy, "Wendy Caishpal, la mujer que convirtió el dolor en fuerza y luz" (2025)

context.heading: From charity to rights
body: The same account describes a 1990s disability movement in El Salvador focused on war survivors' mobility and pensions, and a move after 2000 toward treating disabled people as rights-holders who make their own decisions rather than as objects of charity and medical treatment. Fundación Sendas, profiled on this page, trains disabled people and families in their rights. A person's expectations of a service may come from either history, from neither, or from something else. Ask.

sources.label: Larissa Hotra, Upside Down World, "A Recent History of the Disability Rights Movement in El Salvador" (July 18, 2008)
Fundación Sendas

context.heading: Family and overprotection, in advocates' own words
body: Wendy Caishpal urges families to acompañar sin encerrar, amar sin anular, confiar sin restringir: to support without shutting a person in, love without erasing, and trust without restricting. Jenny Chinchilla says people with disabilities face taboos that come from society and sometimes from their own families. These are the views of two advocates in El Salvador, not findings about Salvadoran families. They offer words that can help when a family's care and a person's own wishes pull apart. Hear the person directly, even if family speaks first.

sources.label: El Diario de Hoy, "Wendy Caishpal, la mujer que convirtió el dolor en fuerza y luz" (2025)
Vórtice, Universidad Francisco Gavidia, "Con el buceo inclusivo, eliminamos barreras" (Dec. 13, 2022)

context.heading: Violence, fear and barriers to care
body: Keller and colleagues interviewed 234 adults at a church shelter in McAllen, Texas, after U.S. border authorities had released them pending a hearing. Of the 234, 114 (48.7 percent) were from El Salvador, and 198 (84.6 percent) were women. In the published report, 191 people (83 percent) cited violence as a reason for leaving, and 119 (69 percent) said they had not reported events to police out of fear of gang retaliation or police corruption. On self-report checklists, 51 people (32 percent) met criteria for post-traumatic stress and 36 (24 percent) for depression. Those percentages rest on fewer than all 234 participants. The sample was recruited at one site and is not representative of Salvadorans in the U.S. or in Minnesota. It suggests a question to ask, not a fact about anyone: fear of authorities may carry over to public agencies.

Zolnikov and colleagues interviewed 20 immigrant Latina women from El Salvador, Guatemala and Mexico who had used mental health services in California. They named barriers including fatalism, gender expectations, stigma, cost, language, threats, abuse and insensitive systems, and they named empathy, advocacy and community approaches as helping. The abstract does not say how many of the women were Salvadoran.
Explain early and plainly who can see a person's information and what it is used for. Say only what your agency's own privacy rules allow.

sources.label: Keller, Joscelyne, Granski and Rosenfeld, PLoS ONE (2017)
Zolnikov, Guerra, Furio, Dennis and Ortega, Dialogues in Health (2023), abstract

context.heading: Temporary Protected Status, as of October 2026
body: Temporary Protected Status for El Salvador was set to expire on September 9, 2026, after a Supreme Court ruling that opened the way to ending TPS designations. Advocates reported on October 9, 2026, that the federal government had not published a formal decision and described the situation as legal limbo. On October 20 they argued that the law extends a designation automatically when no timely decision is made, and they said Salvadoran holders had lost jobs, had trouble renewing driver's licenses and faced barriers to public programs. That is the advocates' account, not a federal notice. This can change quickly, so check the current position with a qualified immigration legal service before advising anyone.

sources.label: MPR News, "What the end of TPS could mean for Salvadorans in Minnesota" (Sept. 8, 2026)
Telemundo, citing EFE, on the end of TPS for Salvadorans (Aug. 14, 2026)
Alianza Americas, press release on TPS legal limbo for Salvadoran families (Oct. 9, 2026)
Alianza Americas and partners, press release calling on DHS to uphold TPS protections (Oct. 20, 2026)

context.heading: Faith and other supports
body: A 2025 conference abstract by Holle reports an online U.S. survey of 154 Latinx parents of children with disabilities, not specific to Salvadorans. The importance parents gave to religious and spiritual beliefs differed by type of disability, with a significant association among parents of children with emotional disabilities. The author suggests social workers may build rapport by including such beliefs in their work, and treats faith communities as places where parents share resources. Involve a congregation only if the person wants that. No source was found on Salvadoran traditional healing for disability, so none is described.

sources.label: Holle, Society for Social Work and Research (2025), conference abstract

context.heading: Older clinical study of Salvadoran refugees
body: A 1991 essay by the anthropologist Janis Jenkins looked at fear and anxiety among Salvadoran refugees who were psychiatric out-patients in North America, in the setting of chronic political violence and poverty. It is one clinical group, decades old. It supports treating distress as connected to what a person has lived through, and it does not tell you how any person will describe their own. No Salvadoran-specific source was found on how the word nervios is used, so no meaning is offered here.

sources.label: Jenkins, Culture, Medicine and Psychiatry (1991)

context.heading: Words and format
body: Salvadoran disability organizations use personas con discapacidad, persons with disabilities, as in the names of the organizations on this page. Older words such as inválido, invalid, carry stigma, and staff should not use them, even if a family does. Follow each person's own preference.
Use trained interpreters, not children. Some Salvadorans are Indigenous, including Nahua/Pipil people, and some speak Indigenous languages. No source was found on disability terms in those languages.

sources.label: Larissa Hotra, Upside Down World, "A Recent History of the Disability Rights Movement in El Salvador" (July 18, 2008)
Fundación Sendas

context.heading: Who is missing
body: No well-documented Salvadoran American disability self-advocate or Minnesota organization led by Salvadoran disabled people was found. Both people and both organizations in this section are based in El Salvador. No Salvadoran-specific evidence was found either on how immigration status affects disability help-seeking, though mixed-status families and fear of systems are raised often. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

sources.label: El Diario de Hoy, "Wendy Caishpal, la mujer que convirtió el dolor en fuerza y luz" (2025)
Fundación Sendas

communityRoutes.name: CLUES Abriendo Caminos Behavioral Health Clinic
communityRoutes.purpose: Behavioral health clinic run by CLUES, a Latino-led nonprofit, at 2600 East 25th Street, Minneapolis. CLUES also runs family, elder and community health programs. Not specific to Salvadorans.

organizations.intro: MPR News reported in September 2026 that more than 14,000 Salvadorans live in Minnesota. An immigration law professor it interviewed said she could not find Minnesota-specific TPS figures and estimated that 3,000 to 4,000 people here would be affected. No Salvadoran association or hometown committee in Minnesota was found, which may mean only that such groups are informal or not online. Organizing that could be documented runs through Latino-led agencies, legal services and the consulate, and, in Greater Minnesota, through Convivencia Hispana in St. James, formed in 2015 with help from Marta Zelaya, who fled El Salvador's war, and which lists roots in Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador. La Prensa de Minnesota, the state's first Spanish-language newspaper, was started in 1991 by a Salvadoran immigrant, Mario Duarte. The list below is a set of starting points for learning, is not complete, and says nothing about who a person trusts.

sources.label: MPR News, "What the end of TPS could mean for Salvadorans in Minnesota" (Sept. 8, 2026)
COPAL MN
MNopedia (MNHS), "La Prensa de Minnesota"

entries.name: Consulate General of El Salvador in St. Paul
entries.location: St. Paul, 60 Plato Boulevard East, Suite 150
entries.purpose: Handles passports, the Salvadoran DUI identity document, and marriage and survival certificates, by appointment through El Salvador's foreign ministry. One of four consular offices added in 2022. These are documents a person may need when applying for services.
entries.linkLabel: Enlace Latino NC guide to Salvadoran consulates

entries.name: Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio
entries.location: St. Paul, 797 East 7th Street; also Minneapolis, Willmar and Austin
entries.purpose: Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio, founded in 1981, calls itself Minnesota's largest Latino-led nonprofit. Programs include behavioral health, career training, children and parenting, elder programs and survivor support. It holds Fiesta Latina each September.

entries.name: COPAL
entries.location: Minneapolis, 2712 East Lake Street; also Mankato and Rochester
entries.purpose: Communities Organizing Latine Power and Action on its own site (Twin Cities Business used the Spanish name Comunidades Organizando el Poder y la Acción Latina in 2024), founded in 2018. Works on organizing and leadership, health and wellness, environmental justice and worker issues, with tenant resources. On September 10, 2026, it published a piece on Salvadoran TPS holders.
aliases: Comunidades Organizando el Poder y la Acción Latina

entries.name: Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota
entries.location: St. Paul, 450 North Syndicate Street, Suite 200
entries.purpose: Immigration legal help for people in Minnesota and North Dakota. TPS is among the issues it lists.

entries.name: Mitchell Hamline School of Law
entries.location: St. Paul, Legal Practice Center, 875 Summit Avenue
entries.purpose: Runs an Immigration Clinic in which students represent non-citizens applying for asylum, VAWA relief, U visas, permanent residence and naturalization, and may also represent clients in deportation proceedings. The clinic's page does not describe how the public can apply for help. Professor Ana Pottratz Acosta, an immigration law expert at the school, explained the end of Salvadoran TPS on MPR News in September 2026.

entries.name: Latino Economic Development Center
entries.purpose: A Latino-focused community development financial institution. Offers entrepreneurs capital, technical assistance and business development help, and supports emerging farmers.

entries.name: Lake Street Council
entries.purpose: Operating as Visit Lake Street, it has supported the Lake Street corridor since 1968 with programs for entrepreneurs, buildings and streetscapes. Sunrise Banks reported in 2026 that the corridor has more than 2,000 businesses and nonprofits. Not specific to Salvadorans.

entries.name: El Rey 94.9 FM
entries.location: West St. Paul, 149 Thompson Avenue East
entries.purpose: Formerly Radio Rey, on WREY. Music, entertainment and news. MPR reported in 2006 that it was founded by a Mexican immigrant and played mostly Mexican regional music, and that it gave airtime to the 2006 immigration rallies. Not specific to Salvadorans.

entries.name: La Prensa de Minnesota
entries.purpose: Started in St. Paul in 1991 by Mario Duarte, a Salvadoran immigrant, as the state's first Spanish-language newspaper. MNopedia says the Duartes sold it in 2006 to El Cine Latino Communications Networks, which later sold it to Latino Communications Network, and that by 2018 it was distributed inside another Spanish-language paper. Covers local, national and international news, including immigration and education.

entries.name: Telemundo Minnesota
entries.purpose: Local Spanish-language news. Listed as KJNK-LD in Meet Minneapolis's media directory.

entries.name: WUMN 21 Minnesota
entries.purpose: WUMN-LD, channel 21, describes itself as a Univision-affiliated station and posts local Spanish-language news.

entries.name: El Minnesota de Hoy
entries.purpose: Daily news for Latinos in Minnesota, covering health, immigration, politics, sports and business.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Founded in 2019. Covers Minnesota immigrants and communities of color, in English. Not specific to Salvadorans.

entries.name: Alianza Americas
entries.purpose: A network of Latin American and Caribbean migrant-led organizations. Issued press releases on TPS for El Salvador on October 9 and October 20, 2026.

entries.name: El Rescate
entries.purpose: Founded in 1981 by the Santana Chirino Amaya Refugee Committee and the Southern California Ecumenical Council. Immigration legal services including asylum, TPS, DACA and citizenship, with free legal clinics by appointment.

entries.name: NALEO Educational Fund
entries.purpose: A nonpartisan nonprofit that helps eligible immigrants with citizenship, mobilizes Latino voters and protects voting rights. Runs a bilingual voting information hotline, 1-888-839-8682.

entries.name: N+ Univision
entries.purpose: National Spanish-language news, including immigration.

entries.name: Telemundo Noticias
entries.purpose: National Spanish-language news, with 2026 coverage of the end of TPS for Salvadorans.

entries.name: elsalvador.com
entries.purpose: Salvadoran national news online, with an international section that covers TPS questions for Salvadorans in the U.S. Publishes El Diario de Hoy's reporting.

entries.name: La Prensa Gráfica
entries.purpose: A Salvadoran national daily, founded in 1915. Covers national news, politics, migration and sports. Its own site is laprensagrafica.com.

entries.name: El Faro
entries.location: Costa Rica, with its newsroom in exile
entries.purpose: Co-founded in 1998 by Carlos Dada and described as the first digital newspaper in Central America. Investigative reporting on El Salvador and Central America. Reporters Without Borders has documented threats and surveillance against its staff. The Committee to Protect Journalists will honor Dada on November 19, 2026.
